He also survives an explosive assassination attempt attributed to the Wolf Pack. During a dungeon expedition, the party defeats enemies that can only be harmed through self-inflicted damage. Joe receives a technical ritual book that points toward alchemically enhanced components, then accepts Jake's offer to train as a Ritualistic Alchemist. In return, Joe must secure guild alignment for Jake and build him a workshop at the future outpost.

Joe gains the Ritualistic Alchemist profession and starts dividing complex ritual work among his coven. An agreement with Daniela lets him study eligible Architects Union buildings, producing many blueprints and rapid Ritual Architect progress. His party also establishes Alexis as alternate leader when he is absent. Joe trains physical characteristics, reaches level 16, gains a magical form of energy sight, and helps raise the Wanderers settlement to town rank two after an organized attack probes its defenses. Boris then reveals a single-use advancement prize near a submerged coastal temple. Sam and his rival party are pursuing the same object. Jess maps the underwater approach with animated scouts, while Joe's coven prepares anchoring and defensive rituals. Poppy reveals a specialization that can isolate opponents in lethal formal duels, and the party enters the flooded dungeon with a dangerous temporary method of breathing underwater. After choosing the wrong historical route, they survive a powerful dwarven automaton, only to learn that Sam's group has breached the final layer and stolen artifacts.

Joe's party confronts Sam's group after the temple breach. Sam surrenders and returns some stolen objects, but secretly keeps another and breaks his oath. Jess steals it back, allowing Joe's party to complete the dungeon and secure a soulbound enhanced advancement tablet. Its extra specialization option remains locked until Joe raises Intelligence and Wisdom to the mortal limit. Joe then discovers that mastering ritual magic's component skills can improve his base class, creating Ritualist Plus and opening a prestige route. While he studies mathematical ritual design, rival guild forces sabotage the Wanderers town and reduce it to rank one. Aten rejects an ultimatum to halt development, survives an internal no-confidence vote, and orders stronger defenses. Joe's coven creates a large structural-repair ritual, and Everard begins teaching Joe polearm combat. Joe also learns that Alexis's increased aggression and paranoia come from a cursed ring. At a temple blockade, high cleric Aaron attacks unlawfully and is nearly killed by the site's neutrality. Joe saves him, and Aaron destroys the ring in repayment.

Inside the Hallowed Lands event, Joe's party competes for the Golden Tome while rising monster strength and forced player battles pressure every group. They find the tome, lose time to Sam's incapacitating attack, recover, and continue fighting for their position. After another difficult victory leaves them exhausted, Sam ambushes and kills the entire party, steals the tome, and causes Joe's quest to fail. The party is barred from the event for a year. Joe still converts event rewards into major class and skill progress, but returns to news that a mass march against the Wanderers is being organized. He and the coven prepare remotely activated defenses as the greenhouse develops dangerous dungeon-like effects. A low-level assault then walks into the town's traps and is destroyed. Public outrage reveals that the attack was designed as propaganda, both exposing the Wanderers' defenses and portraying the guild as needlessly brutal. The guild embraces a tougher defensive stance and rushes development toward town rank three while hostile powers gather.

Joe continues building, crafting, and training while the propaganda campaign raises prices and slows Wanderers development. He makes a ten-year agreement granting Jake exclusive use of an artifact cauldron. In exchange for favorable access and supplies, Joe must build a unique-or-better alchemy workshop at the next-zone outpost within one year. His coven members begin developing separate specialties in blood support, terrain shaping, projectile enchantment, and light effects. Joe studies Ritualistic Forging to stabilize combined rituals. Bard then asks him to add Hansel to the pantheon despite opposition from the Bardic College. The altar releases Hansel, a greater deity associated with bards, teachers, and political assassins. Hansel improves instruction at Pathfinder's Hall, grants Joe perfect fire affinity, and makes Bard his champion with a new specialization. The Bardic College publicly backs the coming assault, drawing more powers into a funded coalition. Joe reveals that Jess and his mother helped him buy supplies through proxies, but he also receives a new obligation to expand greenhouse support from 10,000 to 25,000 people.

The Wanderers complete a unique bathhouse despite a harmful flaw, pushing the settlement to town rank three. The reward includes a once-monthly Town Aegis that protects Wanderers members and town buildings for 24 hours while reflecting double damage. Joe reaches Ritual Architect level 10, but leaves the sealed town to gain the last Luck needed for Aten's plan. He returns to find a million-strong siege force supported by jesters, mage factions, respawn totems, and Architects Guild sappers. Joe infiltrates the army, kills its engineering group, and fights back into town. After bombers breach the wall, Aten names him First Elder in waiting and activates the Aegis. Under its protection Joe kills many attackers, then Aten temporarily raises his characteristics so he can attempt his second specialization.

Four days pass during Joe's specialization trial. He returns after the Aegis has failed, the outer wall has fallen, and surviving Wanderers are trapped in Pathfinder's Hall. Aten's message sends him and Everard to link a prepared quarantine ritual. Joe stages an expulsion from the hall to create room for a later counterattack, links the ritual, and fights through competing enemy factions. He summons a powerful neighbor leader to reach the town core, where Alexis prevents frightened defenders from killing him by mistake. Joe reports that Pathfinder's Hall is ready to counterattack and that all four quarantine rituals are linked and awaiting activation.

At Aten's order, Joe activates the four prepared defenses, unaware that Hannah has used Game Over's blood and removed their safeguards. The intended quarantine becomes an irreversible lethal plague. It persists for nine days and catches at least three million people. It destroys the coalition's siege strategy because twelve war totems funded by Floodwater keep returning attackers into the lethal area. The Wanderers gain the maximum Ruthless title, but survivors turn against Aten. Mr. Banks uses a no-confidence vote to remove him while many members are absent awaiting respawn. Joe invokes his First Elder authority, blocks Banks' takeover, starts the process of restoring Aten, and has Banks expelled into the plague. King Henry's court strips Floodwater of wealth and crown reputation for financing the war. Joe accepts primary responsibility for the catastrophic ritual and is exiled from Midgard for a year and a day. Before leaving, he secretly fills a legendary storage device with guild supplies and spends millions of contribution points on preparations. Aten is re-elected commander. Joe crosses the Bivrost and reaches the next zone, where rival elf and dwarf representatives offer routes to Olfenheim and Svartelheim. Banks' allies later suffer a delayed ritual retaliation hidden in their wine.

characters.description: A poised young woman engaged to her distant cousin Roddy Welman and expecting that they will eventually inherit from their wealthy aunt. An anonymous warning about the aunt's household draws her back to Hunterbury.
characters.name: Elinor Carlisle

characters.description: The Belgian detective, asked to investigate after Elinor Carlisle has already been charged and brought to trial. He is not initially certain of her innocence, but agrees that the evidence is too complete in one direction and examines what the prosecution's neat sequence leaves out.
characters.name: Hercule Poirot

characters.description: Elinor's cousin and fiance at the opening of the story, charming, cultivated, and accustomed to sharing her assumptions about their future and their place in their aunt's affections.
characters.name: Roderick Welman

characters.description: Elinor and Roddy's wealthy aunt, paralysed after a stroke and living at Hunterbury. She is fond of both young relatives and has taken a strong interest in the education and prospects of Mary Gerrard, the lodgekeeper's daughter.
characters.name: Laura Welman

characters.description: The daughter of Hunterbury's lodgekeeper, educated beyond her family's means through Mrs Welman's generosity. Young, attractive, and uncertain where she belongs, she returns from training abroad to find both gratitude and resentment attached to the help she has received.
characters.name: Mary Gerrard

characters.description: The local doctor who attends Mrs Welman. Direct, energetic, and observant, he takes a more personal interest in the people at Hunterbury than his professional manner initially suggests.
characters.name: Dr Peter Lord

characters.description: The district nurse who attends Mrs Welman and knows the Hunterbury household well. Practical and talkative, she shares nursing duties with Nurse O'Brien and has ready access to the routines of the sickroom.
characters.name: Nurse Hopkins

characters.description: An Irish nurse who helps care for Mrs Welman during her final illness. Alert to conversation and domestic detail, she notices more in the sickroom than the family realises.
characters.name: Nurse O'Brien

characters.description: The stern housekeeper at Hunterbury, devoted to the Welman family and resentful of the attention and education given to Mary Gerrard. Her view reflects the local suspicion that Mary has been raised above her station.
characters.name: Mrs Bishop

characters.description: A local young man who knew Mary Gerrard before her education took her away from Hunterbury. He had hoped to marry her and remains hurt and jealous when she returns with broader ambitions and attracts Roddy Welman's attention.
characters.name: Ted Bigland

characters.description: The solicitor handling Mrs Welman's affairs. He explains the legal consequences of her intentions, her existing arrangements, and any will that can or cannot be found.
characters.name: Mr Seddon

recaps.ending: Poirot proves that Nurse Hopkins poisoned Mary Gerrard. The prosecution assumed the morphine was in the fish-paste sandwiches prepared by Elinor, but Hopkins put it into the tea and protected herself by using apomorphine to make herself vomit; the mark on her wrist, explained as a rose-thorn scratch, came from the injection. Hopkins had sent the anonymous letter that brought Elinor and Roddy to Hunterbury and had cultivated knowledge of Mary's parentage and money. She was the relative who stood to benefit under Mary's will, giving her a motive hidden behind the more visible triangle involving Elinor, Roddy, and Mary. The evidence also establishes that Laura Welman's death and the missing morphine supplied Hopkins with knowledge and opportunity, though Elinor's trial concerns Mary's murder. Dr Peter Lord admits that, desperate to save Elinor, he manufactured a line of evidence suggesting another person had been near the lodge; Poirot recognised the fabrication and found the real proof independently. Elinor is acquitted. Her attachment to Roddy is over, and Peter Lord's loyal effort leaves open a quieter future between him and Elinor.
recaps.in_short: Elinor Carlisle and her fiance Roddy Welman visit their invalid aunt Laura at Hunterbury after an anonymous letter warns that the lodgekeeper's daughter, Mary Gerrard, is gaining influence over her. Roddy falls in love with Mary, ending his engagement. Laura dies without a completed will, and Elinor inherits, later making a generous settlement on Mary. At a lunch prepared by Elinor, Mary dies of morphine poisoning, and Elinor is tried with motive, opportunity, and poison all pointing toward her. Dr Peter Lord asks Poirot to investigate. Poirot shows that Nurse Hopkins put morphine in the tea, then used an emetic injection to protect herself. Hopkins had sent the warning letter and was positioned to inherit money Mary left to a relative. Elinor is acquitted; Peter admits that he invented evidence in an attempt to help her, but Poirot's real solution stands. Roddy belongs to Elinor's past, while Peter may belong to her future.

recaps.text: Elinor Carlisle and Roderick 'Roddy' Welman are engaged and expect one day to inherit from their wealthy aunt Laura Welman of Hunterbury. An anonymous letter warns that Mary Gerrard, the lodgekeeper's daughter whom Laura has educated and supported, is persuading the invalid woman to favour her. Elinor and Roddy visit. Laura has suffered a stroke and is attended by Dr Peter Lord, Nurse Hopkins, and Nurse O'Brien. Mary returns from training abroad, attractive and no longer comfortable in the social place assigned to her. The warning may be malicious, but it has identified a real tension around Laura's money and Mary's uncertain standing.

Roddy becomes infatuated with Mary, and his engagement to Elinor breaks under the strain. Laura Welman tries to communicate wishes about her estate but dies before a new will can be completed. Because she dies intestate, Elinor inherits as next of kin. Questions remain about medication in the sickroom and about what Laura meant to arrange for Mary. Elinor conducts herself with outward control despite losing both her aunt and her planned marriage. She decides to sell Hunterbury and makes a substantial financial provision for Mary, an action that is generous but also closes the household in which their lives have become entangled.

As Hunterbury is cleared, Elinor prepares sandwiches for a small lunch with Mary and Nurse Hopkins. Mary eats and soon collapses, dying from morphine poisoning. Elinor had access to morphine from her aunt's sickroom, prepared the food, and had been displaced in Roddy's affections by the victim. Her composure after the death is interpreted as coldness rather than shock. The police build a direct case: opportunity, means, jealousy, and the fact that the other person sharing the meal was not poisoned. Elinor is arrested and sent for trial. Peter Lord, who has developed strong feelings for her, refuses to accept that the visible explanation is the true one.

Peter Lord asks Poirot to examine the case. Poirot makes clear that affection is not evidence and that he will investigate Elinor as seriously as anyone else. He reconstructs Laura Welman's final illness, the medicines in the house, Mary's background, the anonymous letter, and the lunch. The prosecution theory places the poison in food prepared by Elinor, but Poirot tests every item eaten and drunk and asks how one diner could be poisoned while another remained well. He also explores Mary's family connections and the disposition of the money Elinor gave her. Several witnesses offer strong opinions about class, jealousy, and character; Poirot separates those judgements from what each person actually saw.

At trial the case against Elinor appears formidable. Witnesses establish her access to morphine, the broken engagement, the preparation of the sandwiches, and Mary's death soon after the meal. The defence can raise questions but cannot explain the entire sequence. Poirot follows details that do not fit: the precise serving of tea, a small injury on a wrist that has been given an innocent explanation, the possibility of using a drug to empty the stomach, and the financial meaning of Mary's will. He also detects that Peter Lord, driven by desperation, has tried to create an alternative trail involving an unknown person near the lodge. Poirot rejects that false help and prepares evidence that can survive the courtroom without it.

Poirot identifies Nurse Hopkins as Mary Gerrard's murderer. The morphine was not in Elinor's sandwiches but in the tea. Hopkins then used an injection of apomorphine to make herself vomit, explaining why she survived the shared meal; the supposed rose-thorn mark on her wrist was the injection site. Hopkins had sent the anonymous warning that brought Elinor and Roddy to Hunterbury, knew the truth about Mary's family and finances, and was the relative positioned to benefit from Mary's will. She used the obvious jealousy between Elinor, Roddy, and Mary to construct a case against Elinor. Peter Lord admits that he invented evidence of another person's presence in an attempt to save the woman he loves, but Poirot had discarded that fabrication and solved the crime from the meal, the drugs, and the money. Elinor is acquitted. Her relationship with Roddy is finished, while Peter's devotion offers the possibility of a different future.

characters.description: A guarded young woman who has recently settled in Southport, North Carolina, under the name Katie Feldman. She works as a waitress, rents an isolated cottage, owns very little, and avoids questions about the life she left behind.
characters.name: Katie Feldman

characters.description: Katie's friendly neighbor, who lives in the cottage nearest hers. Direct, observant, and easy to talk to, Jo encourages Katie to stop living entirely in isolation and to consider trusting Alex.
characters.name: Jo

characters.description: A widowed former military police officer who runs Southport's general store and raises two young children. Patient and attentive, he recognizes Katie's need for privacy while becoming interested in her.
characters.name: Alex Wheatley

characters.description: Alex's young son. He spends time around the family store, enjoys outdoor activities with his father, and is more reserved than his sister about the changes in their family since their mother's death.
characters.name: Josh Wheatley

characters.description: Alex's young daughter, who is open in her affection and quickly responds to Katie's warmth. Her presence helps draw Katie into the daily life of the Wheatley family.
characters.name: Kristen Wheatley

characters.description: The owner of the Southport restaurant where Katie finds work. He gives her steady employment without pressing her to explain her past.
characters.name: Ivan

characters.description: Katie's husband, a Boston police detective who is searching for the wife he knows as Erin. Possessive and violent, he uses his badge, investigative access, and a misleading account of her disappearance to pursue her after she escapes.
characters.name: Kevin Tierney

characters.description: Alex's late wife and the mother of Josh and Kristen. Alex remembers her as a loving partner who understood that he might eventually need to build a life with someone else after her death.
characters.name: Carly Wheatley

recaps.ending: Kevin tracks Katie to Southport and arrives intoxicated and armed while Alex and his children are with her. He sets the Wheatley store and home ablaze, forcing Katie and the children to escape the fire, and pursues Katie when she draws him away from them. During the violent confrontation, Kevin is killed. Alex, Katie, Josh, and Kristen survive, though their home and business are badly damaged. Afterward Alex gives Katie a letter that his late wife Carly wrote before her death for the woman he might someday love. The letter thanks that future partner for caring for Alex and the children and asks her to help keep Carly's place in their lives. A photograph with the letter shows Katie that Carly was Jo, the neighbor who befriended and advised her, even though no one else had ever met Jo. Katie understands that her friend was Carly's spirit guiding her toward the family. Free from Kevin, she chooses a future with Alex and his children.
recaps.in_short: Calling herself Katie Feldman, Erin Tierney escapes her abusive husband Kevin, a Boston police detective, and builds a quiet life in Southport, North Carolina. She befriends her neighbor Jo and slowly falls in love with widowed storekeeper Alex Wheatley and his children, Josh and Kristen. When Alex realizes she is hiding from danger, Katie tells him about Kevin's violence and the careful escape that brought her south. Kevin abuses police resources to locate her and comes to Southport armed and drunk. He sets fire to Alex's store and home and attacks Katie, but the family escapes and Kevin is killed in the confrontation. Alex later gives Katie a letter written by his late wife Carly to the woman who might one day join their family. A photograph reveals that Carly was Jo, the friend whom only Katie could see. With Carly's blessing and Kevin no longer able to reach her, Katie chooses to remain with Alex and the children.

recaps.text: A young woman calling herself Katie Feldman has recently arrived in Southport, North Carolina. She works long hours as a waitress, rents a remote and sparsely furnished cottage, and saves every small amount she can, while remaining wary of attention. Her nearest neighbor, Jo, is friendly and persistent enough to draw her into conversation. At the town's general store Katie meets its owner, Alex Wheatley, a widower raising his son Josh and daughter Kristen. Alex's background in military police makes him observant, but he does not press Katie when he notices her guarded behavior. Kristen takes to her quickly, and Katie begins returning to the store. These tentative relationships offer her the possibility of belonging, though ordinary kindness still feels dangerous to someone accustomed to planning for escape.

Alex gives Katie a bicycle that will make her journey between the cottage and restaurant easier. She initially reads the gift as an obligation and reacts defensively, but accepts after understanding that he expects nothing in return. Time with Alex, Josh, and Kristen gradually softens her isolation, while Jo encourages her to acknowledge her interest in him. The narrative also reveals the danger behind Katie's caution. Her real name is Erin Tierney, and her husband Kevin is a Boston police detective. At home he subjected her to escalating control and violence, then treated his own suspicions as proof of disobedience. Erin secretly accumulated the means to flee and adopted a new identity. Kevin is now using his professional access to search for her, presenting himself as the wronged husband rather than the source of the threat.

Katie becomes increasingly involved with the Wheatleys. She enjoys the children's trust and sees that Alex remains devoted to the memory of his late wife Carly without being closed to a new relationship. Alex and Katie's attraction develops into love, but his trained eye notices signs that she has altered her appearance and is hiding from someone. Rather than invent another explanation, Katie tells him that she is Erin and describes Kevin's abuse, her fear of the police system surrounding him, and the careful escape that brought her to Southport. Alex believes her and offers practical support without trying to take control of her choices. Katie begins to imagine a future that includes him and the children. Kevin, meanwhile, continues searching, drinking heavily and treating Erin's independence as a personal injury he is entitled to punish.

Katie and Alex settle into a closer relationship, sharing family outings and speaking more openly about both Carly and Kevin. A frightening incident involving the children reinforces their reliance on one another and Katie's attachment to Josh and Kristen. The sense of safety is temporary. Kevin exploits police information and follows the trail Erin worked hard to conceal, eventually identifying Katie's new life in Southport. His thoughts become more disordered as alcohol, jealousy, and a conviction of ownership feed one another. He travels south with his weapon. Katie knows that disclosure has made Alex an ally, but neither of them knows how near Kevin is or how readily he will endanger the children to regain control.

Kevin reaches Southport and watches Katie with Alex and the children, interpreting their happiness as betrayal. Armed and intoxicated, he moves against the family and starts a fire that engulfs the Wheatley store and living quarters. Katie and Alex focus on getting Josh and Kristen out of the burning structure. Katie then draws Kevin away from the children, knowing that she is the object of his pursuit. The confrontation becomes a direct struggle for survival. Kevin's police authority no longer shields him, and the private violence Katie once had to endure without witnesses is exposed as he attacks her amid the destruction he has caused.

Katie resists Kevin during the final attack, and he is killed in the violent confrontation. Alex, Katie, Josh, and Kristen survive the fire, although the store and home are devastated. The end of Kevin's pursuit gives Katie the freedom to choose her life rather than merely hide. Alex later gives her a letter Carly wrote before dying, addressed to the woman he might one day love. Carly asks that woman to care for Alex and the children and to keep her memory present rather than replace it. With the letter is a photograph. Katie recognizes Carly as Jo, the neighbor who befriended her, listened to her fears, and guided her toward Alex, although Alex and the children never encountered Jo. Katie realizes that those conversations were a final act of Carly's care. Receiving her blessing, Katie commits herself to Alex and the children and accepts Southport as home.

characters.description: A teenage peasant from Domremy who arrives at Vaucouleurs certain that Saints Catherine and Margaret, together with the archangel Michael, have ordered her to relieve Orleans and see the Dauphin crowned. Direct, practical, and unwavering, she treats a military campaign as an obvious duty and expects soldiers and nobles to recognize the same necessity.
characters.name: Joan

characters.description: The military commander at Vaucouleurs. Initially exasperated by Joan's repeated requests for armor, a horse, and an escort to the Dauphin, he questions her companions and tests her confidence before allowing her mission to proceed.
characters.name: Robert de Baudricourt

characters.description: A local gentleman and soldier who believes Joan's account of her calling. He supports her request to travel to the Dauphin and is willing to accompany her despite Robert's initial skepticism.
characters.name: Bertrand de Poulengey

characters.description: The uncrowned French heir, uncertain of his legitimacy and intimidated by the debts, courtiers, and military failures surrounding him. He hides among his nobles to test Joan, but her confidence offers him a way to imagine exercising authority rather than avoiding it.
characters.name: Charles VII

characters.description: A senior churchman at the Dauphin's court. Politically cautious and conscious of the Church's authority, he is impressed by Joan's force but wary of accepting a private revelation without examination.
characters.name: Archbishop of Rheims

characters.description: The experienced French commander directing the defense of Orleans. He respects military realities and initially regards Joan as an untrained enthusiast, but he listens when her confidence and the changing conditions give the army a chance to act.
characters.name: Dunois

characters.description: The Bishop of Beauvais, a learned churchman aligned with the English cause. He regards Joan's insistence on answering directly to her voices as a threat to the Church's universal authority and argues that she must be judged for heresy rather than treated merely as a military enemy.
characters.name: Bishop Cauchon

characters.description: The English Earl of Warwick, a courteous but determined political opponent of Joan. He sees her appeal to a united France under its king as dangerous to the feudal order as well as to English power and seeks a lawful means to remove her.
characters.name: Earl of Warwick

characters.description: An English chaplain whose national hatred of Joan is more emotional than theological. He demands punishment in the language of religion while showing little interest in the careful distinctions Cauchon makes about heresy.
characters.name: Chaplain de Stogumber

characters.description: A powerful French noble and soldier at Charles's court. Concerned with practical alliances and his own influence, he has little patience for Joan's certainty or for policies that threaten established interests.
characters.name: La Tremouille

characters.description: The Dominican official who directs Joan's examination at Rouen. Intellectually disciplined and experienced in heresy trials, he presents the court as an effort to return an erring Christian to obedience while steadily narrowing the choices available to her.
characters.name: The Inquisitor

recaps.text: At Vaucouleurs in 1429, amid a period of French defeat, Robert de Baudricourt is baffled by disturbances in his household and by the persistence of Joan, a teenage peasant who has repeatedly demanded an audience. Joan tells him that heavenly voices have ordered her to raise the siege of Orleans and arrange the Dauphin's coronation. She asks for a horse, armor, and soldiers to escort her to court. Robert questions Bertrand de Poulengey and finds that local men have begun to share her confidence. Joan shows no deference to Robert's doubts and treats the military task as both urgent and achievable. Her certainty, along with the response she inspires in others, overcomes his resistance. Even Robert's domestic troubles seem to resolve in her presence, strengthening the impression she makes. Robert supplies what she needs and sends her toward the Dauphin, beginning her movement from an obscure village into the French war.

At Chinon, the uncrowned Charles is surrounded by creditors, factional nobles, and advisers who doubt both his legitimacy and his capacity to rule. To test Joan, he exchanges places with a courtier, but she identifies him among the crowd. In private, Charles admits his fear, lack of money, and wish to escape responsibility. Joan does not solve his political difficulties; instead, she gives him confidence that he has a duty to act as France's king. Her energy shifts the court's mood, although the Archbishop remains cautious about treating her voices as divine authority. The court debates whether she is inspired, naive, or politically dangerous, but its mockery no longer controls the decision. Charles agrees to let her join the campaign for Orleans and accepts coronation at Rheims as a real objective. Joan thus wins official backing without resolving the churchmen's doubts or the nobles' concern about her growing influence.

Outside besieged Orleans, Dunois waits for a favorable wind before moving troops and supplies across the Loire. He respects Joan's courage but explains that determination cannot replace military conditions. When the wind changes, Joan sees it as confirmation of her mission, while Dunois is persuaded less by a miracle than by her ability to turn opportunity into resolve. She insists that the French should attack rather than remain trapped in defensive calculation. The campaign succeeds and the English are driven from Orleans. Her victories alter the war and make her a public symbol. In the English camp, the Earl of Warwick, Bishop Cauchon, and Chaplain de Stogumber consider what she represents. Warwick fears the national loyalty that could weaken feudal rule; Cauchon fears an individual claiming divine direction outside the Church; Stogumber simply wants the English enemy destroyed. They agree that capturing Joan and condemning her through church law will serve their different purposes.

Charles is crowned at Rheims, fulfilling the central promise of Joan's mission, but the ceremony also reveals how far she has moved beyond her allies. Joan wants to continue at once against Paris and complete the military recovery of France. Charles prefers negotiation and the comforts of established kingship; the Archbishop distrusts her independent spiritual certainty; La Tremouille protects political interests; and even Dunois warns that soldiers cannot support her without limit. Joan longs to return to her village but believes her voices require further action. She finds that a victorious symbol is welcome at court only while her demands align with the plans of powerful men. The leaders who benefited from her victories are unwilling to follow her next campaign, and Dunois makes plain that if she is captured he cannot sacrifice the army to rescue her. She nevertheless chooses to continue, accepting an isolation that makes the plans discussed by her English and ecclesiastical enemies increasingly dangerous.

Captured and sold into English hands, Joan is brought before a church court at Rouen. The Inquisitor and Cauchon insist that the issue is not her patriotism but her refusal to submit her voices and judgment to the Church. Joan answers with the same plain certainty that once moved soldiers, but in the courtroom her impatience and literal honesty are turned into evidence against her. The court offers mercy only on terms that deny the authority by which she has lived. When threatened with burning, she signs a recantation. She then learns that obedience will leave her imprisoned for life, deprived of the open world she values. Declaring that her voices and actions were true, she retracts the confession and is condemned as a relapsed heretic. Joan is burned. Ladvenu reports her steadfastness, Stogumber is shattered by seeing the physical cruelty he had demanded, and an English soldier's small kindness at the fire becomes a sign that compassion survived where institutions failed.

Twenty-five years after Joan's death, Charles learns that a new church inquiry has overturned the judgment against her. As he sleeps, Joan appears, followed by allies and enemies from the earlier scenes. Their afterlife conversation measures historical praise against the choices they made while she lived. Cauchon discovers that his defense of church authority did not protect his reputation; Dunois and the others honor Joan without denying that they abandoned her; and the English soldier receives one brief release from damnation for the cross he gave her. A visitor from the twentieth century announces that Joan has been canonized as a saint. The company celebrates the news, but when Joan joyfully asks to return to life, each person retreats behind a reason why her presence would again be inconvenient or dangerous. Alone once more, she confronts the pattern by which society venerates dead reformers while resisting living ones and asks when the world will be ready for its saints.

characters.name: Joan

characters.description: The military captain at Vaucouleurs whose support Joan needs in order to reach the Dauphin. He initially dismisses her mission and threatens to send her back to her father, but becomes unsettled by her certainty and by the way his own soldiers accept her leadership.
characters.name: Robert de Baudricourt

characters.description: Baudricourt's household steward, preoccupied at first by hens that have stopped laying. He reports Joan's long wait for an audience and interprets the household's sudden good fortune as evidence that she should be taken seriously.
characters.name: The Steward

characters.description: A young soldier who believes Joan is inspired and is willing to accompany her through dangerous territory to the Dauphin. His confidence in her helps demonstrate to Baudricourt that she already commands the loyalty of fighting men.
characters.name: Bertrand de Poulengey

characters.description: The uncrowned French heir, burdened by debt, an uncertain claim, and a court that has little faith in him. characters.name: Charles VII

characters.description: A senior churchman and political adviser at the Dauphin's court. He is initially suspicious of Joan's claimed voices and conscious of the disorder an unauthorized visionary may cause, though he also recognizes the force of hope she brings to a demoralized cause.
characters.name: The Archbishop of Rheims

characters.name: La Tremouille

characters.description: A nobleman at the Dauphin's court whose conspicuous blue beard gives him his familiar name. He participates in the attempt to confuse Joan by letting another courtier pose as the Dauphin.
characters.name: Bluebeard

characters.description: The experienced French commander defending Orleans. He welcomes Joan's effect on morale but expects military decisions to answer to weather, supply, and professional judgment. Their first encounter tests whether her conviction can coexist with his command.
characters.name: Dunois

characters.description: An English nobleman determined to preserve England's claims in France. He regards Joan's victories as a dangerous political force that turns local loyalties toward a French nation, and he seeks a lawful way to remove her without presenting the matter as simple military revenge.
characters.name: The Earl of Warwick

characters.description: The Bishop of Beauvais, a learned French churchman aligned with the English side. characters.name: Peter Cauchon

characters.description: An English chaplain whose fierce patriotism makes him demand punishment for Joan as an enemy and supposed witch. Less intellectually controlled than Warwick or Cauchon, he gives open voice to the hatred surrounding the proposed trial.
characters.name: John de Stogumber

characters.description: A Dominican official who directs the examination of Joan. Calm and formidable, he sees her not as a simple impostor but as a sincere person whose refusal to submit her revelations to the Church makes her more, rather than less, dangerous in his eyes.
characters.name: The Inquisitor

characters.description: A young Dominican assigned to counsel Joan during the trial. He urges her to accept the Church's guidance and later offers the human comfort available to her within a proceeding whose course he cannot control.
characters.name: Brother Martin Ladvenu

recaps.ending: After Joan is burned at Rouen, the epilogue moves to Charles VII's bedroom twenty-five years later. Ladvenu reports that a formal review has overturned the verdict against her, and Joan appears in Charles's dream. The dead and aging people connected with her case arrive in turn. Some praise her, some apologize, and Cauchon learns that later generations condemned him despite his conviction that he served the Church. An English soldier is briefly released from hell because he gave Joan a small cross at the stake. A modern cleric announces that Joan will be canonized in 1920. When Joan asks whether she should return to life now that the world calls her a saint, her admirers recoil from the practical cost of having her among them again and disappear. Left alone, she asks when the world will be ready to receive its saints. Her reputation has been repaired, but the final scene shows that admiration after death does not mean society would tolerate the living independence for which she was destroyed.

recaps.text: At Vaucouleurs, Captain Robert de Baudricourt is troubled by military setbacks and by a strange domestic failure: his hens have stopped laying. A teenage peasant named Joan has waited persistently to see him. She says saints have ordered her to lift the siege of Orleans and have the Dauphin crowned at Reims, and she demands soldiers, armor, and a horse for the journey. Baudricourt initially calls the claim madness, but Joan already has the confidence of Bertrand de Poulengey and other men who volunteer to escort her. Her direct assurance, the men's loyalty, and the sudden report that the hens are laying again overcome his resistance. He grants her request and sends her toward the royal court.

Joan reaches the Dauphin's court at Chinon, where Charles is weak, indebted, and unsure of his right to rule. The courtiers disguise another man as the Dauphin, but Joan identifies Charles and speaks with him privately. She gives him enough courage to accept her mission, overcoming resistance from political and church advisers who doubt either her voices or the practicality of her plan. At Orleans, she meets the commander Dunois while French forces wait for a favorable wind to cross the Loire. Joan insists on immediate action and rebukes the caution that has settled over the army. When the wind changes, Dunois accepts the event and her effect on the soldiers as grounds to follow her. The French attack with renewed confidence, placing Joan at the center of the campaign.

Joan answers a long interrogation with courage and common sense, but the judges demand that she submit her voices and choices to church authority. Threatened with immediate burning, she signs a recantation and is sentenced to perpetual imprisonment. The sight breaks Stogumber's certainty and exposes the cruelty behind his earlier demands for punishment.

A cleric from the twentieth century arrives to announce Joan's canonization. The company enthusiastically praises a safely dead saint. When Joan asks whether she should come back to life, however, each person finds a reason to retreat. Alone again, Joan recognizes that later honor has not made the world ready to live with a person who challenges its institutions as she did.

characters.description: A young squirrel of Redwall Abbey who admires Martin the Warrior and longs to prove that he can be brave. Energetic, impulsive, and handy with a sling, he treats adventure as a game until events beyond the Abbey demand more of him.
characters.name: Samkim

characters.description: A young molemaid at Redwall and Samkim's close friend. Her broad dialect and cheerful appetite disguise a practical traveller with courage, common sense, and the digging skill of her species.
characters.name: Arula

characters.description: An otter living at Redwall Abbey, known for his strength, endurance, and readiness to help. He is dependable in a crisis and more comfortable acting than debating.
characters.name: Thrugg

characters.description: A very young dormouse in Redwall's care. Small enough to be carried by an adult traveller, he is curious, trusting, and unexpectedly resolute when separated from the safety of the Abbey.
characters.name: Dumble

characters.description: The badger ruler of Salamandastron and commander of its fighting hares. A formidable warrior with a fierce temper, he has raised Mara as his daughter but struggles to temper his protectiveness with the freedom she wants.
characters.name: Urthstripe the Strong

characters.description: Urthstripe's adopted badger daughter, raised inside Salamandastron under the close watch of its lord and Long Patrol. Strong-willed and restless, she resents being treated as a child and wants to see the world beyond the mountain.
characters.name: Mara

characters.description: A young hare of Salamandastron and Mara's devoted companion. Talkative, hungry, and outwardly light-hearted, he follows her lead even when her plans take them beyond the mountain's protection.
characters.name: Pikkle Ffolger

characters.description: A blue-eyed weasel warlord whose horde advances on Salamandastron. He cultivates a calm, reasonable manner while using poison, deception, and sudden violence to remove anyone in his way.
characters.name: Ferahgo

characters.description: Ferahgo's son, a young weasel who shares his father's blue eyes and ambition. Clever, vain, and impatient to command, he watches for any chance to advance himself within the horde.
characters.name: Klitch

characters.description: A veteran hare sergeant of Salamandastron's Long Patrol. Blunt, disciplined, and loyal to Urthstripe, he helps hold the mountain's defenders together as danger approaches.
characters.name: Sapwood

characters.description: A stoat who deserts Ferahgo's horde with his companion Thura. Hungry, dishonest, and chiefly interested in staying alive, he heads east through Mossflower without understanding all that he carries with him.
characters.name: Dingeye

characters.description: Dingeye's fellow deserter from Ferahgo's army. He is a shabby opportunist who follows his companion toward Redwall in search of food and shelter.
characters.name: Thura

characters.description: The leader of a travelling band of Guosim shrews. Suspicious of strangers but bound by loyalty once friendship is established, he commands skilled boatbeasts and fighters.
characters.name: Log-a-Log

recaps.ending: Ferahgo's assault reaches Salamandastron, where the Long Patrol, the returning travellers, and their allies fight beside Urthstripe. The badger lord confronts the Assassin in the mountain heights, and their final struggle carries both of them to their deaths. Klitch escapes the battle but does not escape the consequences of his father's treachery; he dies while fleeing. The horde breaks, and Salamandastron survives at heavy cost. Mara returns after learning what lay behind Urthstripe's severity, and she and the surviving hares mourn him with a better understanding than they had when she ran away. At Redwall, Thrugg's northern journey secures the Flowers of Icetor, allowing the Abbey to overcome Dryditch fever. Samkim and Arula return having carried Martin's sword through real danger rather than the imagined adventures with which they began. The separate roads end in recovery at Redwall and peace at the mountain, though both communities remember those lost to the sickness and war.
recaps.in_short: As the weasel assassin Ferahgo marches a horde toward the badger stronghold of Salamandastron, Lord Urthstripe's adopted daughter Mara rebels against his strict protection and runs away with the hare Pikkle. At Redwall Abbey, two deserters from Ferahgo's army bring the deadly Dryditch fever and steal Martin the Warrior's sword. The young squirrel Samkim and molemaid Arula pursue them west, while the otter Thrugg travels north with the infant dormouse Dumble to find the rare Flowers of Icetor needed for a cure. These journeys gather allies and eventually converge around the besieged mountain. The flowers save Redwall, and the returning wanderers help Salamandastron's Long Patrol resist Ferahgo. In the final battle Urthstripe and Ferahgo die together, Klitch dies during his escape, and the horde collapses. Mara returns with a better understanding of her adoptive father and mourns him, while Samkim and Arula bring Martin's sword safely home after earning the responsibility they once only imagined.

recaps.text: Redwall Abbey stands in Mossflower as a peaceful home whose creatures preserve the sword and memory of Martin the Warrior. Far to the west, Salamandastron is a mountain stronghold traditionally ruled by a badger and defended by fighting hares. This story introduces a new generation at both places and does not require the outcome of an earlier Redwall tale.

Two dangers begin far apart. Ferahgo the Assassin, a blue-eyed weasel whose courtesy conceals a talent for poison and betrayal, leads a large horde toward Salamandastron. The mountain is ruled by Urthstripe the Strong, a badger warrior whose adopted daughter Mara is increasingly angered by his attempts to control her. Mara and her hare friend Pikkle decide to leave the mountain and find freedom for themselves. At Redwall Abbey, the young squirrel Samkim and molemaid Arula dream of adventures beyond the walls, with little idea of their cost.

Mara and Pikkle are now travelling beyond Salamandastron, while Urthstripe's anger at their departure adds to the pressure of preparing the mountain against Ferahgo. The Assassin advances carefully, using scouts, threats, and internal rivalries to keep his horde obedient; his ambitious son Klitch is among those waiting for weakness. In Mossflower, Ferahgo's deserters Dingeye and Thura reach Redwall. Their arrival links the distant war to the Abbey even though its residents do not yet understand the danger.

Dingeye and Thura rob Redwall and flee with Martin the Warrior's sword. Samkim and Arula go after them, changing an idle wish for adventure into a dangerous journey west. The stoats have also brought Dryditch fever into the Abbey. As the illness spreads, Redwall's healers learn that their best hope is the Flowers of Icetor, a rare plant found far to the north. Thrugg the otter undertakes the search, with the infant dormouse Dumble caught up in the expedition. Redwall is left fighting sickness while its travellers head in opposite directions.

Samkim and Arula continue west with Martin's sword at the centre of their pursuit, meeting creatures whose help has to be earned rather than assumed. Their road begins to draw them toward Salamandastron and the war gathering there. Mara and Pikkle discover that life outside the mountain is not the simple freedom they imagined; they face deception and captivity before finding allies among the Guosim shrews. Thrugg and Dumble press into the northern country for the cure as Redwall's fever worsens behind them. At Salamandastron, the Long Patrol prepares to withstand a much larger attacking force.

The separate journeys begin to turn back toward their threatened homes. Thrugg reaches the country where the Flowers of Icetor can be found and must survive the hazards guarding the cure before carrying it south. Samkim and Arula recover Martin's sword and travel with new allies toward the western mountain. Mara and Pikkle, now accompanied by shrews, also move back toward Salamandastron with a harder understanding of the world outside it. Ferahgo closes his grip around the mountain, probing the Long Patrol's defences while Urthstripe prepares for a battle that cannot be avoided.

Thrugg's expedition returns with the Flowers of Icetor, giving Redwall the means to halt Dryditch fever and save the creatures who remain ill. In the west, the travellers and their allies reach Salamandastron as Ferahgo's siege becomes a direct assault. Mara returns to the home she rejected and learns more of the fear and love behind Urthstripe's harsh protection. Samkim and Arula arrive no longer playing at heroism, and Martin's sword becomes part of the mountain's defence. The Long Patrol and its allies hold against Ferahgo's horde, but the struggle is narrowing toward a personal reckoning between the Assassin and the badger lord.

The allied defenders break Ferahgo's attack on Salamandastron. Urthstripe confronts the Assassin in the mountain heights, and the two enemies fall to their deaths in their final struggle. Ferahgo's son Klitch escapes the battlefield but dies while fleeing, undone by the legacy of his father's treachery, and the surviving horde scatters. Mara and the Long Patrol are left to mourn Urthstripe and rebuild the peace he died defending. At Redwall, the Flowers of Icetor overcome Dryditch fever. Samkim and Arula return with Martin's sword after proving themselves through endurance and responsibility, while Thrugg and Dumble come home from the northern quest. Redwall and Salamandastron survive, each marked by losses but secure again.

characters.description: The young princess of Judaea, daughter of Herodias and stepdaughter of Herod. She leaves the royal banquet for the terrace, where the imprisoned prophet's voice draws her attention. Accustomed to being obeyed, she is fascinated by what is forbidden to her.
characters.name: Salome

characters.description: A prophet held in a cistern beneath Herod's palace. His declarations condemn the ruling household, especially the marriage of Herod and Herodias. Herod fears his spiritual authority, while Herodias wants him silenced.
characters.name: Jokanaan

characters.description: The ruler of Judaea, husband of Herodias and stepfather of Salome. Troubled by omens and by Jokanaan's preaching, he nevertheless keeps the prophet imprisoned rather than surrendering him to his enemies. His attention toward Salome is possessive and unwelcome.
characters.name: Herod

characters.description: Salome's mother and Herod's wife. Jokanaan publicly condemns her marriage, and she resents both his accusations and Herod's fixation on her daughter.
characters.name: Herodias

characters.description: The young captain of Herod's guard. Deeply infatuated with Salome, he watches her during the banquet and yields when she asks him to disobey Herod's order by bringing Jokanaan out of the cistern.
characters.name: Narraboth

characters.description: A companion of Narraboth who notices the danger in the captain's obsessive attention to Salome. He repeatedly warns Narraboth and reads the strange appearance of the moon as an omen.
characters.name: The Page of Herodias

recaps.ending: Bound by the oath he made before his guests, Herod reluctantly orders Jokanaan's execution after Salome refuses every substitute for the prophet's head. The head is brought from the cistern on a silver shield. Salome addresses it and kisses its mouth, completing the desire that Jokanaan rejected while alive. Herod is appalled by the spectacle. He first orders the palace lights extinguished, but moonlight reveals Salome still absorbed in the severed head. Unable to tolerate what he sees, he commands his soldiers to kill her. They advance together and crush Salome beneath their shields. Jokanaan, Narraboth, and Salome are all dead; Herod and Herodias remain in power, but the banquet has ended in the violence foreshadowed throughout the play.
recaps.in_short: At Herod's palace, Princess Salome becomes fascinated by Jokanaan, the imprisoned prophet who condemns her mother Herodias's marriage to Herod. Narraboth, the young guard captain infatuated with Salome, brings Jokanaan from his cistern for her. The prophet rejects Salome's advances, and Narraboth kills himself in despair. Later Herod begs Salome to dance and swears to grant any reward. After performing, she demands Jokanaan's head. Herod offers jewels and power instead, but Salome will not change her request, and Herod orders the execution. Salome receives the severed head and kisses it. Horrified, Herod commands his soldiers to kill her, and they crush her beneath their shields.

recaps.text: During a banquet at Herod's palace, Salome leaves the hall to escape her stepfather's attention. On the terrace she hears Jokanaan, a prophet imprisoned in a cistern for denouncing Herod and Herodias. Salome persuades Narraboth, the guard captain who adores her, to bring the prisoner out. She becomes consumed with desire for Jokanaan, but he rejects her and returns below. Narraboth, unable to bear the encounter, kills himself. Herod and Herodias come outside, arguing over omens, the prophet, and Herod's interest in Salome. Herod asks Salome to dance and publicly promises her any reward. She performs, then demands Jokanaan's head on a silver shield. Herod offers riches, sacred objects, and political favors instead, but she refuses every substitute. Trapped by his oath, he authorizes the execution. When the head is brought up, Salome addresses it and kisses its mouth. Herod reacts with horror and orders the lights put out; seeing her still illuminated by the moon, he commands his soldiers to kill her. They crush Salome beneath their shields, ending the banquet in violence.

characters.description: The blinded Israelite champion held captive in Gaza after revealing the secret of his strength. Once empowered to fight the Philistines, he now performs forced labor and regards his defeat as the consequence of his own disobedience. His physical power has begun to return, but he is burdened by shame, isolation, and uncertainty about whether he can still serve a divine purpose.
characters.name: Samson

characters.description: A group of Israelite men from Samson's tribe who come to lament with him during a Philistine festival. They question the meaning of his rise and fall, respond to each visitor, and frame his suffering within the hopes of an oppressed people.
characters.name: Chorus of Danites

characters.description: Samson's elderly father, grieving his son's blindness and captivity. He has retained hope, resources, and a practical plan to negotiate Samson's release, even while struggling to understand how a life announced by divine promise reached such misery.
characters.name: Manoa

characters.description: Samson's estranged Philistine wife, whose persistent questioning led him to disclose the source of his strength and enabled his capture. She comes richly dressed to seek forgiveness, explaining her betrayal in terms of fear, love, and loyalty to her people, and offers to care for him if he will accept her.
characters.name: Dalila

characters.description: A celebrated Philistine warrior from Gath who visits Samson to taunt him. Proud of his stature and military reputation, he treats Samson's captivity as proof of Philistine superiority while avoiding the captive's proposal that they settle the boast in single combat.
characters.name: Harapha

characters.description: A Philistine official sent to order Samson to perform feats of strength at the festival honoring Dagon. He presents the summons as a command backed by the rulers of Gaza and returns with threats when Samson initially refuses.
characters.name: Philistine Officer

characters.description: A witness who reaches Manoa and the Chorus after a terrible crash interrupts their waiting. Shaken by what he has seen, he reports the destruction at the Philistine festival and explains Samson's part in it.
characters.name: Messenger

recaps.ending: Samson goes to the festival after sensing that the summons may offer a final purpose. In the theater he performs for the assembled Philistine rulers, then asks to rest against the building's two central pillars. Calling on God for strength, he pulls the supports down. The structure collapses, killing Samson along with the Philistine lords, priests, warriors, and other spectators gathered around him. A messenger brings the news to Manoa and the Chorus, who understand that Samson has destroyed more enemies in his death than during his life. Manoa mourns his son but does not regard the death as disgraceful. He plans to recover Samson's body, return it to the family burial place, and honor him with a monument. The Chorus closes by finding a severe form of consolation in the outcome: Samson's captivity has ended, the Philistine leadership has suffered a devastating blow, and an event that seemed incomprehensible has reached a completed purpose.
recaps.in_short: Blind and enslaved in Gaza, Samson laments that he squandered a divinely granted strength by revealing its condition to his Philistine wife, Dalila. A Chorus of Danites mourns with him. His father Manoa hopes to ransom him; Dalila seeks reconciliation and is rejected; and the warrior Harapha taunts him but declines a direct contest. A Philistine officer orders Samson to display his strength at a festival for Dagon. Samson first refuses, then senses an inward prompting and agrees to go. While Manoa pursues plans for his release, a great crash is heard. A messenger reports that Samson asked to rest between the theater's supporting pillars and pulled the building down, killing himself and the assembled Philistine rulers and worshippers. Manoa resolves to bury him with honor. The Chorus interprets the catastrophe as the completion of Samson's mission: his personal disgrace ends in a final act against the power holding him and his people captive.

recaps.text: During a festival for the Philistine god Dagon, the blinded Samson is allowed a day of rest from forced labor in Gaza. He laments the choices that led to his capture: although set apart to deliver Israel and granted extraordinary strength, he disclosed the condition of that gift to his Philistine wife, Dalila, who betrayed him. A Chorus of Danites joins him and tries to understand his fall. Samson's father, Manoa, arrives with hopes of paying a ransom, but Samson doubts that release can repair his disgrace. Dalila then asks forgiveness and offers to tend him; Samson rejects both her explanations and her offer. The Philistine champion Harapha comes to boast over the captive, yet refuses Samson's challenge to fight. An officer summons Samson to entertain the Philistine rulers with feats of strength at their festival. Samson initially refuses to take part in worship he rejects, but after the officer returns with threats, he senses an inward prompting and goes. Manoa returns with plans for his release, only for a great crash to be heard. A messenger reports that Samson performed before the assembly, rested against the theater's central pillars, and pulled them down, killing himself and the gathered Philistine elite. Manoa resolves to recover and honor his body, while the Chorus finds consolation in a mission completed through death.

characters.description: A girl living with her father and younger brother on a prairie farm. She remembers the songs and warmth of her mother, who died after Caleb was born, and watches carefully as Sarah arrives in answer to Papa's advertisement. Thoughtful and protective, she narrates the family's cautious hope that Sarah might stay.
characters.name: Anna Witting

characters.description: Anna's younger brother, born shortly before their mother's death. Curious, direct, and hungry for stories about the parent he cannot remember, he openly asks the questions Anna is reluctant to voice and quickly hopes Sarah will become part of their family.
characters.name: Caleb Witting

characters.description: Anna and Caleb's widowed father, a prairie farmer who has raised them alone since his wife's death. Quiet and capable, he places an advertisement for a wife and corresponds with Sarah Wheaton, inviting her to visit the farm for a month before either of them makes a permanent promise.
characters.name: Jacob Witting

characters.description: A woman from the coast of Maine who answers Jacob's advertisement and agrees to come west for a trial visit. She describes herself as plain and tall. Independent, practical, and affectionate, she loves the sea, sings old songs, draws, and wants to learn the work of the prairie rather than be treated as a guest.
characters.name: Sarah Wheaton

characters.description: Sarah's brother in Maine, with whom she has been living before answering Jacob's advertisement. His approaching marriage helps prompt Sarah to seek a new home, and Sarah's memories of him remain tied to the family and ocean she has left behind.
characters.name: William Wheaton

characters.description: The Wittings' neighbor and Matthew's wife. Friendly and reassuring, she welcomes Sarah into prairie life and understands the difficulty of leaving one landscape and family for another.
characters.name: Maggie

characters.description: A neighboring farmer and Maggie's husband. He helps Jacob with the practical cooperation farm families need from one another across the open prairie.
characters.name: Matthew

recaps.ending: Sarah learns to drive the wagon and then goes to town alone. Because she has spoken so often of missing Maine and the sea, Anna and Caleb fear that she has used the trip to leave them. Sarah returns at dusk carrying practical supplies as well as colored pencils for the family. She explains that missing the sea does not mean she wants to abandon the prairie: if she left, she would miss Jacob, Anna, and Caleb even more. Her return answers the question that has troubled the children throughout her visit. Sarah has chosen their family and intends to stay, allowing them to look ahead to her marriage to Jacob and to a home shaped by both her coastal memories and their prairie life.
recaps.in_short: Widowed prairie farmer Jacob Witting advertises for a wife, and Sarah Wheaton writes from Maine before agreeing to visit for a month. Jacob's children, Anna and Caleb, want her to stay but fear she will miss the sea too much. Sarah arrives with shells, songs, drawing paper, and her cat. She joins the farm's work, learns to ride and drive, teaches the family songs, and tries to make the prairie home her own while speaking honestly about the coast she loves. After a severe storm, she proves that she will face hardship alongside them. When she later drives to town alone, the children think she may be leaving. Sarah returns with supplies and colored pencils and tells them that although she misses the sea, she would miss Jacob, Anna, and Caleb more. She has chosen to stay and become part of their family.

recaps.text: Anna and her younger brother Caleb live with their widowed father, Jacob, on a prairie farm. Their mother died after Caleb was born, leaving Anna with memories of her songs and Caleb with questions about the woman he never knew. Jacob places a newspaper advertisement for a wife. Sarah Wheaton answers from Maine, where she has lived with her brother William near the sea. In letters exchanged with Jacob and the children, Sarah describes herself as plain and tall, asks about the family and farm, and says she sings. She agrees to visit them for a month so they can decide whether they suit one another. Anna and Caleb begin imagining her arrival, hopeful that she will bring singing back to the house and anxious that she may decide not to remain.

Sarah arrives from Maine wearing a yellow bonnet and bringing her cat, Seal, along with gifts from the coast. She gives the children shells and lets them listen for the sound of the sea, then begins learning the rhythms of the farm. She is warm but direct, and she does not pretend that the prairie resembles the home she left. Sarah sings and draws, tells Anna and Caleb about swimming in the ocean, and shows an eagerness to participate in outdoor work. The children study every sign of whether she is happy. Caleb asks openly if she will stay, while Anna worries more quietly that the flat, dry landscape cannot compete with Sarah's love for Maine.

Sarah becomes more fully involved in farm life. She befriends their neighbor Maggie, who also understands what it means to make a home far from one's original family. Sarah learns to ride Jacob's horse and wants to learn to drive the wagon herself, insisting on competence and independence. She helps repair the roof and shares work with Jacob rather than remaining inside the house. Yet she continues to miss the sea and tries to preserve it through pictures, colors, shells, and songs. Anna and Caleb grow increasingly attached to her, so every reference to Maine renews their fear that her visit is temporary and that the household will become quiet again when she leaves.

A fierce storm strikes the farm. The family shelters together, and Sarah helps protect the animals and face the damage, demonstrating that she will share the difficult parts of prairie life as well as its pleasures. Later she learns to drive the wagon and goes into town alone. Anna and Caleb become convinced that she may be leaving for Maine, especially when she is gone for hours. Sarah returns at dusk with household supplies and colored pencils. She tells them that she will always miss the sea, but that if she left the prairie she would miss Jacob, Anna, and Caleb even more. By returning of her own choice, she resolves the children's fear: she intends to stay and make a life with their family.

characters.description: The unnamed first-person observer at a lavish Parisian ball given by the Lanty family. Standing between the warm celebration indoors and the wintry garden outside, he becomes fascinated by a strange elderly guest and later explains the family's history to his companion.
characters.name: The Narrator

characters.description: A fashionable young widow who attends the Lantys' ball with the narrator. Her curiosity about the family's wealth and their secretive elderly relative prompts the narrator to tell her the history of Sarrasine and La Zambinella.
characters.name: Madame de Rochefide

characters.description: A gifted and passionate French sculptor who studies under Bouchardon and travels to Rome. Captivated by the opera singer La Zambinella, he mistakes an artistic ideal for a complete knowledge of another person, and his refusal to accept the truth leads to his death.
characters.name: Ernest-Jean Sarrasine

characters.description: An eminent sculptor who recognizes Sarrasine's talent, takes him on as a pupil, and imposes discipline on the difficult young artist. His training helps Sarrasine win recognition and travel to Italy.
characters.name: Bouchardon

characters.description: A celebrated Roman opera singer whom Sarrasine believes to be a woman and loves as the living embodiment of beauty. La Zambinella is actually a castrato, since women were barred from the Roman stage. In old age, this same person is the mysterious relative protected by the wealthy Lanty family.
characters.name: La Zambinella

characters.description: A wealthy patron who protects La Zambinella. His social circle encourages Sarrasine's mistaken courtship as entertainment, but his men intervene decisively when the sculptor threatens the singer.
characters.name: Cardinal Cicognara

characters.description: The beautiful daughter of the Lanty household, admired at the Parisian ball for her grace and musical talent. Her family's mysterious wealth is bound to the secret history of their elderly relative, La Zambinella.
characters.name: Marianina de Lanty

characters.description: A member of the wealthy Lanty family and one of the elegant young figures at their ball. The family's intense protection of its elderly relative helps create the mystery that draws the narrator and Madame de Rochefide into the old story.
characters.name: Filippo de Lanty

recaps.ending: Sarrasine abducts La Zambinella after learning that the singer he loves is a castrato. Feeling that both his desire and his artistic ideal have been betrayed, he threatens to kill La Zambinella, but agents of Cardinal Cicognara stab Sarrasine first. A statue Sarrasine made from the singer's image later passes through the Lanty family and indirectly influences another famous representation of ideal beauty. The narrator reveals that the uncanny old guest at the Lantys' ball is La Zambinella in extreme old age and that the family fortune derives from this relative. Madame de Rochefide reacts to the story with disgust and disillusionment, distancing herself from both love and the narrator. The frame closes with beauty, wealth, and desire all shadowed by the concealed history behind them.
recaps.in_short: At a ball hosted by the rich and secretive Lanty family, an unnamed narrator and Madame de Rochefide notice a frail, uncanny old guest. The narrator explains the mystery through the story of Sarrasine, a talented French sculptor who went to Rome and became obsessed with the opera singer La Zambinella. Believing the singer to be a woman, he treated La Zambinella as both beloved and artistic ideal. He eventually learned that Roman restrictions kept women from the stage and that La Zambinella was a castrato. Sarrasine abducted and threatened the singer, then was killed by Cardinal Cicognara's men. The old guest at the ball is La Zambinella decades later, and the Lantys' fortune comes through this hidden family connection. The revelation repels Madame de Rochefide and ends the narrator's hope of intimacy with her.

recaps.text: At the Lanty family's opulent Parisian ball, the unnamed narrator watches the contrast between the lively rooms and the frozen garden. He and Madame de Rochefide are intrigued by a very old, almost spectral guest whom the family carefully shields from attention. To explain the figure, the narrator tells of Ernest-Jean Sarrasine, a rebellious but brilliant sculptor trained by Bouchardon. In Rome, Sarrasine sees the opera singer La Zambinella and falls in love, imagining that the performer perfectly embodies feminine beauty. Members of Cardinal Cicognara's circle encourage his error, while La Zambinella gives warnings he does not understand. Sarrasine finally discovers that the singer is a castrato, women having been excluded from the Roman stage. He abducts La Zambinella and, enraged at the collapse of his romantic and artistic ideal, threatens murder. Cicognara's men kill Sarrasine. The narrator identifies the old guest as La Zambinella and explains that the Lanty fortune comes through this concealed relative. Madame de Rochefide responds with revulsion and rejects the narrator's romantic approach, leaving the revelation to darken the beauty and wealth of the ball.

characters.description: A successful London neurosurgeon in his late forties. He is disciplined, observant, and accustomed to explaining behavior through the workings of the brain. During a single Saturday, disturbances in the city and an accidental confrontation test his confidence that professional skill and an orderly family life can keep danger at a distance.
characters.name: Henry Perowne

characters.description: Henry's wife, a newspaper lawyer. Her demanding career has not weakened the warmth of their marriage, and Henry thinks of her as the emotional center of their household.
characters.name: Rosalind Perowne

characters.description: Henry and Rosalind's adult daughter, a poet who is returning from Paris with the first copies of her newly published collection. She is politically engaged and often argues with her father, especially over the approaching war in Iraq.
characters.name: Daisy Perowne

characters.description: Henry and Rosalind's teenage son, an accomplished blues guitarist preparing for an evening performance. Music gives him an absorbing vocation and a perspective less argumentative than either his father's or his sister's.
characters.name: Theo Perowne

characters.description: Rosalind's father, a celebrated poet living in France. He is proud, competitive, and a powerful influence on Daisy's writing, although their shared vocation also gives them reasons to quarrel.
characters.name: John Grammaticus

characters.description: Henry's elderly mother, once a strong competitive swimmer and now living in residential care with advanced dementia. Henry's visits confront him with a decline that even his medical knowledge cannot reverse.
characters.name: Lily Perowne

characters.description: An American anesthetist who works with Henry and is also his regular squash opponent. Their friendship includes intense competition on the court and practiced cooperation in the operating theatre.
characters.name: Jay Strauss

characters.description: A young man whose car has a minor collision with Henry's near the anti-war march. Aggressive and volatile in front of his companions, he also shows small involuntary movements that Henry recognizes as possible signs of a serious neurological disorder.
characters.name: Baxter

characters.description: One of the men accompanying Baxter after the traffic collision. His presence strengthens the threat facing Henry during what began as an ordinary exchange of insurance details.
characters.name: Nigel

recaps.ending: Baxter survives his fall but needs urgent brain surgery. Henry returns to the hospital and operates on him with Jay Strauss, repairing the injury despite knowing that Baxter invaded his home and threatened his family. Henry chooses not to pursue revenge and expects that Baxter will face legal consequences while also confronting the degenerative illness Henry identified. Back at home, Daisy's pregnancy has become family knowledge, and the danger has drawn the Perownes together rather than breaking them apart. Henry finds Rosalind awake, and they briefly recover the intimacy with which their marriage began. He finally returns to bed near dawn, ending the same Saturday on which he woke. The wider political questions that occupied him remain unresolved, but the day has forced him to recognize both the fragility of his protected life and the limited, practical forms of care he can still provide.
recaps.in_short: On 15 February 2003, London neurosurgeon Henry Perowne wakes before dawn and sees a burning aircraft descend toward Heathrow, an image that feeds his anxiety about terrorism and the coming Iraq war. The city is filling with an enormous anti-war march when a diverted journey leads to a collision with Baxter, a violent young man whose symptoms Henry recognizes as Huntington's disease. Henry escapes the confrontation by exploiting that knowledge, then continues a day of squash, errands, and a visit to his mother. That evening his wife Rosalind, children Daisy and Theo, and father-in-law John gather for dinner. Baxter and an accomplice invade the house, humiliate the family, and threaten violence. Daisy's recitation of a poem unexpectedly moves Baxter; Henry and Theo then overpower him, causing him to fall down the stairs. Henry later operates on Baxter's injured brain. Returning home near dawn, he accepts both the vulnerability of his family life and his continuing duty to preserve life, even that of the man who attacked them.

recaps.text: Before dawn on Saturday, 15 February 2003, Henry Perowne wakes in his London townhouse and watches a burning aircraft descend toward Heathrow. Reports eventually suggest a mechanical emergency rather than an attack, but the sight connects with his unease about terrorism, Iraq, and the uncertain world beyond his comfortable life. His wife Rosalind sleeps while he reflects on their marriage and their children: Daisy, a newly published poet due home from Paris, and Theo, a gifted young blues musician. The family also expects Rosalind's father, the poet John Grammaticus, for dinner. Henry talks with Theo, follows the news, and prepares for his usual squash match with his colleague Jay Strauss. Outside, central London is filling with crowds for the huge demonstration against military action in Iraq, a cause that Daisy supports and about which she and Henry disagree.

Police diversions around the anti-war march send Henry down an unfamiliar route, where his car clips another vehicle. Its driver, Baxter, and two companions make the minor accident threatening. Henry notices Baxter's jerky movements and quickly infers that he has Huntington's disease, an inherited degenerative condition. By speaking as a doctor and hinting at treatment, Henry isolates Baxter from his companions and avoids a beating, but he has also exposed a private fear and humiliated the younger man. Henry then plays a fiercely contested squash match with Jay, losing after an argument over the final point. The encounter with Baxter continues to trouble him even after he has escaped the immediate danger.

After the squash match, Henry shops for the family's dinner and visits his mother Lily in her care home. Her dementia has stripped away much of their shared history, leaving him able to offer attention but no cure. He returns home and prepares a fish stew while the family converges. Daisy arrives with her poetry collection, Theo performs with his blues band, and John Grammaticus joins them. Old tensions surface: Daisy and her grandfather compete over poetry, while she and Henry resume their dispute over Iraq. Henry's opposition to Saddam Hussein is complicated by the suffering of an Iraqi patient he once treated, though he remains uncertain that invasion is justified. Daisy privately reveals to her mother that she is pregnant, news not yet shared with Henry. Their disagreements remain affectionate, and Henry feels the strength of the domestic world he has built, unaware that the roadside confrontation has not ended.

Baxter and Nigel enter the Perownes' home and hold the family at knifepoint. Baxter strikes John and forces Daisy to remove her clothes, exposing her pregnancy to everyone.
